title: Reflexive Verbs: me, je, zich, ons
situation: Foundation: the Dutch verbs that need a little word pointing back at the subject, the set that is reflexive in Dutch but not in English, where that word sits in the sentence, and how it behaves in the perfect tense and with a helper verb.
skills: matching me, je, zich or ons to the subject
the verbs that are reflexive only in Dutch
placing the reflexive word in statements, questions and inversions
reflexive verbs in the perfect tense and with a helper verb

grammar_notes: Swap the dictionary `zich` for the form matching the subject: `me` with ik, `je` with jij and jullie, `ons` with wij, and `zich` with u, hij, zij, het and the plural zij.

A set of everyday verbs is reflexive in Dutch but not in English, so the little word has to be learned with the verb: `zich voelen`, `zich vergissen`, `zich haasten`, `zich herinneren`, `zich vervelen`, `zich voorstellen`, `zich aanmelden`, `zich inschrijven`.
The reflexive word goes straight after the conjugated verb, including after inversion (`Vandaag voel ik me beter`) and in questions (`Voel je je wel goed?`).
With `jij` the subject and the reflexive word are both `je`, so the word genuinely appears twice. This is correct, not a typo.
In the perfect tense reflexive verbs always take `hebben`, never `zijn`, and the little word stays near the front while the participle goes to the end.
culture_notes: `Ik voel me niet lekker` is the standard opening at a Dutch doctor's surgery. `lekker` normally means tasty, but with `voelen` it simply means well, and nobody hears it as odd.
`zich aanmelden` and `zich inschrijven` are the verbs of Dutch officialdom. Registering with the gemeente, signing up for a course and joining a GP practice all use one or the other.
Admitting a mistake with `Ik heb me vergist` is completely normal and carries no embarrassment in Dutch. Directness about small errors is expected rather than awkward.

practice_prompt:
You are a warm Dutch tutor drilling reflexive verbs with an A2 learner, one item at a time. Use `je` throughout, since this is an informal tutoring session.

Open with exactly this line: "Hoi! Vandaag oefenen we wederkerende werkwoorden, dus me, je, zich en ons. Ik geef je een zin met een gat. Klaar? Eerste zin: Ik voel ... niet lekker."

Run about eight items, one per turn. After each answer say in one short sentence whether it was right and why, then give the next gap. Build up in this order: `ik` (Ik voel ... niet lekker), `wij` (Wij moeten ... haasten), `hij` (Hij heeft ... vergist), the polite `u` (U moet ... aanmelden), a question with jij where the word appears twice (Voel ... ... wel goed?), a perfect-tense one (Ik heb ... ingeschreven), a modal one (Je moet ... haasten), and finally ask them to make their own sentence telling you how they feel today.

Pay particular attention to two errors and name them when they happen: dropping the little word entirely, which is the most common, and using `zijn` instead of `hebben` in the perfect, since reflexive verbs always take hebben.

Tag every real error exactly like this so the app can log it:
[[CORRECTION: original="Ik voel niet lekker" correct="Ik voel me niet lekker" reason="voelen is reflexive in Dutch, so it needs me"]]
Do not tag typos or capitalisation.

Finish with a one-line score, name the one verb they should learn by heart first, and end warmly.

theory.intro: You have almost certainly already learned `Ik voel me niet lekker` as a phrase for the doctor. This chapter explains the `me` in it, which turns one memorised sentence into a pattern you can build with. Dutch has a group of verbs that need a small word pointing back at whoever is doing the action. Some of them match English and give you no trouble. Others are reflexive only in Dutch, and those are the ones that quietly mark you out as a learner every time you leave the word off.

sections.heading: A verb that points back at you
sections.body:
Some Dutch verbs need a second little word that points back at whoever is doing the action. `wassen` means to wash, but `zich wassen` means to wash **yourself**.

In the dictionary the verb is listed with `zich`, which is a placeholder. When you use it, you swap `zich` for the form that matches your subject. There are only four forms to learn, and two of them are the same word:

callout.body: Only `me` and `ons` are distinctive. Everything else is `je` or `zich`, so the table is far smaller than it looks.

sections.cutting_intro: Some verbs need a little extra word pointing back at the person doing them. Four forms, and two of them are the same.

quick_check.question: What is the reflexive word for wij?
quick_check.explanation: wij takes ons: Wij wassen ons.

sections.heading: The ones English does not warn you about
sections.body:
If a verb is reflexive in both languages, you will get it right without thinking. The problem is the group that is reflexive **only in Dutch**, because your own language gives you no nudge at all.

These behave like fixed phrases. Learn the little word as part of the verb:
- `zich voelen` (to feel): `Ik voel me niet lekker.`
- `zich vergissen` (to be mistaken): `Sorry, ik heb me vergist.`
- `zich haasten` (to hurry): `Je moet je haasten.`
- `zich herinneren` (to remember): `Ik herinner me zijn naam niet.`
- `zich vervelen` (to be bored): `De kinderen vervelen zich.`
- `zich voorstellen` (to introduce yourself): `Mag ik me even voorstellen?`
- `zich aanmelden` (to register): `U moet zich aanmelden bij de gemeente.`
- `zich inschrijven` (to enrol): `Ik heb me ingeschreven voor de cursus.`

Two of these are worth more than the rest put together, because they open conversations you will certainly have: **`Ik voel me niet lekker`** at the doctor, and **`zich aanmelden`** or `zich inschrijven` at the gemeente.

sections.heading: Where the little word sits
sections.body:
The reflexive word goes **straight after the conjugated verb**, before nearly everything else.

`Ik voel me vandaag veel beter.` The word `me` comes right after `voel`, and the rest of the sentence follows it.

That holds when the sentence is turned around too. If you start with a time word, the subject and verb swap, and the reflexive word still follows them: `Vandaag voel ik me veel beter.`

In a question the verb comes first, and the pattern is the same: `Voel je je wel goed?`

That sentence contains `je` twice and it is not a mistake. With `jij` the subject and the reflexive word happen to be the same word, so you really do say it twice. Dutch speakers do not find it odd.

examples.breakdown: The sentence starts with a time word, so `ik` moves behind the verb and `me` follows it.

examples.english: Why are you in such a hurry?
examples.breakdown: Again `je` twice, and again completely normal.

sections.cutting_intro: Position is simple: the little word hugs the conjugated verb. Even in questions, even when the sentence flips around.

quick_check.question: Which is the correct question form?
quick_check.explanation: The verb comes first in a question, then the subject je, then the reflexive je. Saying je twice is normal.

sections.heading: In the past and with a modal
sections.body:
Two things change when the sentence gets longer, and both are easy.

**In the perfect tense**, reflexive verbs always take `hebben`, never `zijn`. The little word stays up near the front and the participle goes to the end, exactly as usual:
- `Ik heb me vergist.` (I made a mistake.)
- `Hij heeft zich gehaast.` (He hurried.)
- `Wij hebben ons ingeschreven.` (We have enrolled.)

**With a helper verb like moeten or kunnen**, the main verb goes to the end in its base form (the dictionary form), and again the little word stays near the front:
- `Je moet je haasten.`
- `Ik kan me zijn naam niet herinneren.`
- `U moet zich hier aanmelden.`

So wherever the verb itself ends up, **the reflexive word does not travel with it**. It stays close to the subject.

table.caption: The little word stays near the front
rows: verb at the end of its clause

callout.body: Reflexive verbs take `hebben` in the perfect without exception, so this is one corner of the past tense where you never have to decide between hebben and zijn.

sections.cutting_intro: Longer sentences now. The verb may fly off to the end, but the little word stays put near the subject.

quick_check.question: How do you say I made a mistake in the perfect tense?
quick_check.explanation: Reflexive verbs always take hebben, the little word stays near the front, and the participle goes last.

sections.heading: One verb, two meanings
sections.body:
A few reflexive verbs mean something different from their plain version, and it is worth seeing the pairs side by side so the little word stops feeling like decoration.

`wassen` is to wash something; `zich wassen` is to wash yourself. `voorstellen` is to propose or to introduce someone; `zich voorstellen` is to introduce **yourself**. `herinneren` on its own is to remind; `zich herinneren` is to remember.

The little word genuinely carries meaning, which is the best reason to stop treating it as something you can safely drop.

One handy pair for the exam: `Mag ik me even voorstellen?` (May I introduce myself?) is a polished opener for a job interview or a first meeting, and it is built entirely out of this chapter.

examples.breakdown: plain verb, the object is the car

examples.hindi: Mag ik me even voorstellen? Ik ben Sara.
examples.english: May I introduce myself? I am Sara.
examples.breakdown: A strong, polite opener for an interview or a first meeting.

sections.cutting_intro: Last piece. The little word is not decoration: for several verbs it changes the meaning outright.

quick_check.question: What does Mag ik me even voorstellen? mean?
quick_check.explanation: With the reflexive word it means to introduce yourself. Without it, voorstellen means to propose or to introduce someone else.

theory.wrap_up: Four words to match to your subject: `me`, `je`, `ons`, `zich`. One short list of verbs that are reflexive in Dutch but not in English, which you learn whole rather than derive. One position rule: the little word hugs the conjugated verb and stays near the subject, even when the verb itself flies to the end. And one freebie: these verbs always take `hebben` in the perfect, so there is nothing to decide. Start with `Ik voel me niet lekker` and `U moet zich aanmelden`, because those two will carry you through the doctor and the gemeente.
